title: ROAD OILING
full_story:

title: COUNTY ARRESTS
full_story:
At about 7 pm Sunday evening, Wayne County deputies responded to a report of a female being battered in the front yard of a residence in Fairfield.  Police arrived and learned their suspect, Preston M. Slone, 27 of Dix had fled on foot.  Deputies pursued Slone and took him into custody after a brief chase.  Slone was arrested and booked into the Wayne County jail on charges of domestic battery and resisting arrest.

Quanden L. Boblet, 29 of Xenia was arrested last Friday, after a Wayne County deputy was dispatched to a report of an unresponsive man inside his vehicle.  On arrival, police were able to wake Boblet and assisted him out of his vehicle.  During a conversation with the suspect, he became aggressive and took a fighting stance.  Police quickly detained him and took him to jail.  Boblet has been booked into the county jail on charges of drunk driving.

Gage L. Devers, 29 of Sims was arrested Sunday, on a White County warrant charging him with driving on a suspended or revoked license.  He was held pending transfer to White County.

Also, Cody R. McKinney, 34 of Rinard was arrested Saturday night in Carmi, on a White County warrant charging him with theft over $500.  McKinney turned himself in at the White County Sheriff’s Department lobby shortly after 9:30 pm.  After booking, he was released with pretrial conditions.

title: CROP PROGRESS AND CONDITION
full_story:
Harvest is right around the corner for many Illinois farmers.  In its latest crop progress and condition report released yesterday, the USDA estimated 4% of the state’s corn is mature and 2% of soybeans are dropping leaves.

According to the USDA there were 4.3 days suitable for fieldwork in the week ending August 23rd.  Statewide, the average temperature was 73.6 degrees, .3 degree above normal.  Precipitation averaged .92 inches, 0.11 inches above normal.  Topsoil moisture supply was rated 3% very short, 10% short, 68% adequate, and 19% surplus.  Subsoil moisture supply was rated 5% very short, 13% short, 67% adequate, and 15% surplus.

Corn dough reached 90%, compared to the 5-year average of 86%.  Corn dented reached 47%, compared to the 5-year average of 50%.  Corn mature reached 4% compared to the 5-year average of 3%.  Corn condition was rated 4% very poor, 8% poor, 30% fair, 43% good, and 15% excellent.

Soybeans setting pods reached 90%, compared to the 5-year average of 87%.  Soybeans dropping leaves are at 2% compared to the 5-year average of 1%.  Soybeans condition was rated 4% very poor, 8% poor, 29% fair, 46% good, and 13% excellent.

title: COMMUNITY CHOIR REHEARSALS
full_story:
For 16 seasons, the Olney Central College Community Choir has brought together singers from across Southeastern Illinois to share their voices, build friendships and experience the joy of making music together.

OCC Director of Choral Activities Dr. Andrew Pittman invites new and returning singers to become part of the tradition when rehearsals begin at 6 pm on September 8th.

“There is something special about making music together,” he said.  “To share the joy of singing together and to experience that visceral sense of connection that happens when voices come together is truly unique.”

The choir offers an opportunity for fellowship and camaraderie while giving singers the chance to learn, grow and perform alongside others who share a love of music.  High school-age singers and older are welcome to participate, and no audition is required.  The only requirements are the ability to carry a tune and, most importantly, a desire to sing.

“I think one of the most rewarding things about the Community Choir is seeing people come in at the beginning of the semester and watching their confidence grow,” Pittman added.

Rehearsals will be held from 6 to 8 pm on Tuesdays in Room 216, the OCC Choir/Band Room, on the second floor of Dr. Kent L. Wattleworth Hall.  The choir will present its annual Christmas Concert at 7 pm on December 3rd in the Dr. John D. Stull Performing Arts Center.

To register for the OCC Community Choir, call 618-395-7777 as soon as possible.

title: ISP OREP PATROLS
full_story:
Illinois State Police (ISP) Troop 9 Commander, Lieutenant Bruce Waggoner, announced that the ISP will conduct Occupant Restraint Enforcement Patrols (OREP) in Effingham, Wayne, Fayette, Marion, White, and Wabash counties during August and September.  OREPs allow the ISP to focus on safety belt and child safety seat laws.  Illinois law requires all vehicle passengers, front and back, to be buckled up.

Safety belts are still one of the most effective safety devices in vehicles, estimated to save over 14,000 lives each year.  Nearly 50% of vehicle occupants killed in traffic crashes were not buckled up.  The objective of this program is to increase occupant restraint compliance through education, child safety seat inspections, and enforcement.

title: MAIL IN BALLOTS
full_story:
Illinois voters can apply to vote by mail for the November 3rd general election.

Illinois voters may request a mail-in ballot for any reason.  The deadline to request a ballot is October 29th.

Voters can request a mail-in ballot by completing an application.  Applications are available by visiting Clay County Clerk Amy Britton’s office in the Clay County Courthouse in person or through the Illinois State Board of Elections website.

Completed applications should be returned to the clerk’s office.

title: GRAYSON DIES
full_story:
The former Sangamon County Sheriff’s deputy convicted of shooting an unarmed woman in the face after she called for help died Sunday morning, his attorney confirmed.

Sean Grayson, who was 32, died after serving less than a year of his 20-year prison sentence, defense attorney Dan Fultz said.

Grayson shot Sonya Massey, 36, while she was in her kitchen on July 6, 2024, after she called 911 to report a prowler outside her home.  Grayson responded with another deputy, whose body camera recorded the events leading up to the shooting.  That video showed Grayson shooting the unarmed Massey.

Sangamon County State’s Attorney John Milhiser reviewed the video and the Illinois State Police investigation and charged Grayson with first-degree murder 11 days after Massey’s death.

Grayson’s attorneys confirmed in court documents that doctors diagnosed Grayson with colon cancer in 2023, before Massey’s shooting, but shared that the cancer had then spread to his liver and lungs.

While in the county jail awaiting trial, records obtained by Capitol Illinois News showed that Grayson was transported regularly to Springfield for medical treatment.

At Grayson’s trial, he appeared gaunt and thin, much thinner than the deputy who was 6-foot-4 and weighed 225 pounds at the time of the shooting.

In May, Grayson requested a compassionate release under the Joe Coleman Act.  In his petition, Grayson claimed that Massey invited him into her home and then attacked him with a boiling pot of water.  Sonya Massey’s family opposed the release.

The Illinois Prisoner Review Board denied his request in late July.

The Illinois Department of Corrections did not respond to an email regarding Grayson’s death on Sunday.  Grayson was in IDOC’s custody at the time of his death but details about his detention were never released.

title: AIDE ARRESTED
full_story:
A Carbondale Community High School teacher’s aide allegedly cultivated an online relationship with an underage girl, sending her money and gifts while repeatedly encouraging her to make sexually explicit videos of herself, according to a federal criminal complaint and an FBI affidavit.

Austin Knoob, 32, of Carbondale, who is also the former owner of Levels nightclub, faces two counts of sexual exploitation of a child.  He pleaded not guilty last week in federal court in Benton.  Judge Reona Daly on Monday denied Knoob’s pretrial release; he will remain in custody while his case is pending.

The case originated in Boston and quickly led to Knoob’s arrest after he admitted to the FBI that he had been talking to the girl, who said she was 12 when they first met online, according to a sworn affidavit filed last week by FBI Special Agent Samuel J. Sukovich, who investigates violent crimes against children from the FBI’s Marion office.

Later, Knoob allegedly recruited the girl into an online group whose members encouraged her to share videos of her harming herself.  She was then added to an even more extreme group she described as a “cult” that included members sharing videos of people committing suicide and other bizarre acts, the affidavit alleged.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Casey Bloodworth asked the court to keep Knoob in custody, saying the allegations against him suggest a “deep-seated, heavily rooted sexual deviancy.”  While the government’s charges involve one minor victim, Bloodworth said there may be additional victims identified as the investigation unfolds.

Knoob’s attorney said Knoob did not have a prior record, noting he would use an ankle monitor and said his dad had offered to ensure he had no internet access. But Judge Daly sided with the government in keeping him in custody, saying that despite hearing numerous child pornography cases, “I have never seen anything like this.”

The girl was interviewed July 28, and the FBI’s Boston office referred the investigation to agents in Marion on Aug. 6. Six days later, agents interviewed Knoob at his home. Knoob, who the girl knew as “Frank” online, was taken into custody two days later.

Carbondale Community High School Superintendent Daniel Booth said Knoob was hired as an aide in August 2025 and resigned effective April 10, one day after the text exchange underlying the second federal charge.  The period documented in the affidavit largely overlaps with his employment at the high school.

The FBI encouraged anyone with information to report concerning Knoob to contact the bureau at 1-800-CALL-FBI and make a report, referring to this specific incident.

title: CLEAR EYES RECALL
full_story:
The Food and Drug Administration reported that bottles of Clear Eyes Maximum Itchy Eye Relief have been voluntarily recalled over potential contamination.

According to the FDA notice, the 0.5-fluid-ounce bottles were distributed nationwide by Medtech Products, which is owned by Prestige Consumer Healthcare in New York.

No other eye drops were included in the recall and no injuries have been reported to date, according to a Prestige spokesperson.  “Although the affected product was not confirmed to be contaminated, we initiated this voluntary recall out of an abundance of caution and our commitment to providing consumers with safe, high-quality products,” the spokesperson said in an email.

The eye drops are sold over the counter nationwide at major retailers.

The 39,060 recalled products were labeled Lot 2552A, with a recall number of D-0766-2026 and expiration date of September 30th, 2027.  The recall began July 29th and is ongoing.

The FDA notice listed the recall as Class II, meaning there may be temporary or medically reversible health problems.  The reason for the recall was “lack of assurance of sterility,” the notice said.
